entries.title: Cubs 3B Alex Bregman's team-bonding trip to Churchill Downs is a rousing success
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — For the Cubs’ off day Thursday, third baseman and race-horse owner Alex Bregman helped organize a team trip to Churchill Downs. It ended up being a wonderful bonding experience, and he made a little bit of money, to boot.</p><p>Bregman’s horse Act of Parliament won his first race in four career starts, taking a maiden claiming race by less than a length in front of the whole team — including reliever Ryan Rolison, who was dressed as a horse. More on that later.</p><p>The trip had been planned for a month. Within that time, Bregman Family Racing bought Act of Parliament, who went to post in the final race of the night. The atmosphere at the track was far from what it is on Derby Day, at least until the dark bay colt rallied to win in an 11-horse field.</p><p>The Cubs celebrated wildly in the winner’s circle and hoisted jockey Axel Concepcion as though he had hit a walk-off home run. Act of Parliament paid out $8.68 off a $2 bet to win, and he earned Bregman, who has raced horses since 2022, $27,108 of the $48,000 purse. Act of Parliament got claimed, though, likely ending his time in Bregman’s stable.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr"><a href="https://x.com/a_concepcion16?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@a_concepcion16</a> gets it done for <a href="https://x.com/ABREG_1?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ABREG_1</a> and the <a href="https://x.com/Cubs?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Cubs</a> ✅ <a href="https://t.co/57bX3rWY1A">pic.twitter.com/57bX3rWY1A</a></p>— Churchill Downs (@ChurchillDowns) <a href="https://x.com/ChurchillDowns/status/2100762275028074818?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But the payout wasn’t the point of the trip. The Cubs flew into Louisville, Kentucky, on Thursday, the day before opening a three-game series against the Reds about 100 miles away, for the purpose of coming together away from baseball at a pressure-packed time of the season.</p><p>“It was a great time,” Bregman said. “We had all the guys out there. It was a lot of fun to be able to share that experience with them. Just being around the group this time of year is super important, just building a camaraderie.”</p><p>Bregman shared much of the experience on Instagram. He showed a video of center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong petting Act of Parliament before the race with the caption, “PCA pep talk we couldn't lose.”</p><p>“I just think it’s good that you get the whole group together, having fun,” said Bregman, who has had plenty of fun himself since the All-Star break, entering Friday with a 1.007 OPS and 17 home runs in 56 games. “It’s what it’s all about, building that team chemistry. That was probably a core memory for me right there doing it with this group of guys.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Off day W courtesy of <a href="https://x.com/ABREG_1?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ABREG_1</a>’s horse at <a href="https://x.com/ChurchillDowns?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ChurchillDowns</a>. 🐎 <a href="https://t.co/jC40JhFvQG">pic.twitter.com/jC40JhFvQG</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2100789335482155222?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>That includes Rolison, who got stuck wearing a silly horse costume for opening his big mouth in a pitchers meeting a month ago. Manager Craig Counsell was there, and he revealed the plan for the off day. Some veterans said the trip would be a good time a rookie dress-up day.</p><p>“Thank God I don’t have to do that anymore, because I had to do it last year,” Rolison said.</p><p>Replied Counsell: “You don’t get to decide when you’re a rookie.”</p><p>So even with more than two years of service time, Rolison was a rookie again.</p><p>“It was good fun,” he said. “I’m a big personality in the clubhouse. So they gave me the horse, and everyone else was jockeys. I embraced it.”</p><p>And the Cubs embraced each other, which is a good sign for a team looking to get on a roll before the posteason. They entered Friday with their magic number for a playoff spot at four, meaning they could have it wrapped up this weekend.</p><p>When they walked into the visitor’s clubhouse at Great American Ballpark, they were met by wet carpet and an odor of beer and champagne, remnants of the Dodgers’ celebration for winning yet another division title Thursday. Could that smell of victory inspire the Cubs this weekend?</p><p>“It just smells in there, to be honest with you,” Counsell said.</p><p>It sounds like the Cubs will have to channel their joy from Churchill toward their playoff push.</p><p>“What are the chances, we plan this trip, and Bregman buys a horse, and it’s the last race of the night and the horse wins?” Rolison said. “You can’t script it out any better. It was a great team-bonding off day.”</p>

entries.title: Nazareth's defense dominates Providence, which loses its first game after firing Tyler Plantz
entries.summary: <p>Two teams facing a midseason gut-check met up on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/17/high-school-football-scores-week-5" >Friday</a> in LaGrange Park.</p><p>No. 5 Providence spent the past week in a media firestorm after the school <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/14/tyler-plantz-providence-football-fired" >fired head coach Tyler Plantz</a>. The unusual mid-season <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/13/providence-fires-football-coach-tyler-plantz" >coaching change</a> caught the attention of casual sports fans and the local television media.</p><p>For Nazareth, the problems this season have all been on the field. The Roadrunners were highly touted in the preseason but lost three of their first four games. The defeats were to good teams, and Nazareth is missing several of its top players to injuries, but the season risked heading down a negative path with another loss.</p><p>“Our two senior captains have been injured, and we have had a lot of adversity against us,” Nazareth receiver Jackson Flickenger said. “We had meetings all this week about staying together, and we took that super seriously.”</p><p>The No. 22 Roadrunners dominated defensively and pulled out a 17-7 victory. It was Providence's first loss of the season, now helmed by interim head coach Adam Nissen, previously the team’s offensive coordinator.</p><p>Nissen acknowledged before the game that a loss was likely to fan the flames of controversy that started on Sunday when Providence announced Plantz’s firing. But he isn’t worried about how his team will handle the defeat internally.</p><p>“Our senior group is awesome,” Nissen said. “I have no doubt we will bounce back. We will watch some film and get ready. We will be ready next week.”</p><p>The Celtics (4-1) had a chance to cut the deficit to one possession when they recovered an onside kick with 8:40 left, trailing 17-7.</p><p>But junior defensive lineman John Bukovac stepped up with a big sack on the next play. And junior linebacker Harry Keenan grabbed an interception on fourth down with just more than a minute to play that sealed the win.</p><p>“We had to stay locked in as a team and trust each other and get it done,” Keenan said.</p><p>Sean Trayser and Henry Walz had interceptions for Nazareth in the first half.</p><p>“The defense was excellent,” Roadrunners coach Tim Racki said. “Especially with the weapons Providence has. Their running game is lethal.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Second INT of the game for Nazareth. Henry Walz grabs the tipped pass. <br><br>Roadrunners and Providence scoreless in the 2Q. <a href="https://t.co/I5XaGiCYQn">pic.twitter.com/I5XaGiCYQn</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2101093396979097924?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>But Nazareth’s running game stole the show. Charles Calhoun put the Roadrunners (2-3) ahead 17-0 with a six-yard TD run to cap off a drive that sucked up most of the third quarter.</p><p>“That was like a 10-minute drive,” Calhoun said. “I could feel it. We were on a roll. Once we get on a high, there is no taking us down.”</p><p>Calhoun had 24 carries for 103 yards, and Jack Parisi added 14 carries for 77 yards.</p><p>Nazareth quarterback JJ Chapman was 7-for-16 passing for 89 yards. He threw a 34-yard touchdown pass to Charles Heck late in the first half. Flickenger had five catches for 42 yards.</p><p>“We really came to play a complete football game,” Racki said. “And that is hard to do after an emotional loss last week. Our kids had an edge all week.”</p><p>Providence running back Broden Mackert had 17 carries for 123 yards and one touchdown. Celtics quarterback Dominic Vita went 13 of 20 for 90 yards with three interceptions.</p><p>“We definitely knew they had been through some adversity this week with their coach being fired,” Calhoun said. “We came out hard. We knew it would be a game to fight for and we wanted to use that to our advantage.”</p><p>Nazareth limited media access to the game, and no television cameras or independent videographers were present.</p><p>Otherwise, it was business as usual for Providence despite all the controversy around Plantz’s firing. A handful of Celtics fans in the crowd wore white T-shirts that read “We support coach Plantz.”</p><p>“We left too many plays on the field,” Nissen, who was previously a head coach at St. Laurence, said. “A couple turnovers; didn’t execute like we normally do. We had a good week of practice and were pretty locked in on what we were trying to do. We had the opportunities at the end of the game; we just couldn’t capitalize on it.”</p>

entries.title: Gaby Domercant looking forward to next adventure at DePaul Prep
entries.summary: <p>For pretty much her whole life, Gaby Domercant has embraced new adventures.</p><p>A couple of more are on tap.</p><p>After sitting out last season following her transfer from Young, Domercant is preparing for her senior basketball season at DePaul Prep. And the season after that, she’ll be off to play college ball at Iona after recently committing to the Gaels.</p><p>‘‘I really prayed about it a lot and I really connected with the staff on my visit,’’ Domercant told the Sun-Times. ‘‘They have a lot of dexperience, so that was something I really valued. And they’ve been winning. They’ve been super-successful in the [Metro] conference already.’’</p><p>Iona was one of 17 Division I scholarship offers for Domercant, a 5-9 guard. Through the recruiting process, she had the advice of her parents, both of whom were Division I athletes. Dad Henry is now a Bulls assistant after playing at Naperville North and Eastern Illinois before a long career overseas. Mom Alexandra played volleyball at Eastern Illinois.</p><p>‘‘My dad thought I was going into the volleyball pipeline . . . but I just fell in love with basketball and he couldn’t keep me away,’’ Domercant said jokingly.</p><p>That love for the game grew when Domercant was living in Russia, Turkey and Italy during her dad’s playing days.</p><p>‘‘Basketball has taken our family all over the world,’’ she said. ‘‘I was super-grateful for all of those experiences.’’</p><p>That globetrotting has given her a perspective that’s rare for a teenager.</p><p>‘‘I remember Turkey the most because I went to grade school there,’’ Domercant said. ‘‘My best friend was Turkish. I went to an English preschool, [and] we would go on all these crazy field trips. . . . All of those kids were learning English, so we were able to communicate a little bit.’’</p><p>Now she’s ready to embark on another adventure at DePaul Prep.</p><p>The Rams went 22-7 and reached a Class 4A regional final last season, but they graduated two Division I recruits in 6-2 Grace Lee (Boston University), the program’s career scoring leader, and 6-2 Kaitlin Totaro (Loyola-Maryland).</p><p>Domercant has expanded her skills since the last time she played high school basketball as a sophomore at Young in 2024-25.</p><p>‘‘I know a lot of people know me as someone who would stand there and shoot,’’ she said. ‘‘I’m trying to expand my game to do other things and contribute in other ways.’’</p><p>DePaul coach Corey Morgan said he is eager for others to see this new version of Domercant, who isn’t going to completely change her identity.</p><p>‘‘She’s an amazing shooter, a dynamic scorer,’’ Morgan told the Sun-Times. ‘‘She immediately fit right in. She knew most of the girls from the community and the neighborhood.’’</p><p>And she’ll be a big part of whatever success the Rams have this season.</p><p>‘‘We are guard-driven and guard-loaded,’’ Morgan said. ‘‘Her shooting is going to allow us to stretch the court. We don’t have two 6-2 kids [anymore]. We’re going to try to get<br>after some people.’’</p>

entries.title: Music venue expected to be centerpiece of $7 billion development project near United Center
entries.summary: <p>Details of the new 6,000-seat music venue planned around the United Center as part of a $7 billion privately funded redevelopment project were released on Friday.</p><p>The Music Hall, which is intended to “create a new type of music experience” in Chicago, is scheduled to open in 2028. Its design is meant to center live performances, unlike other Chicago venues, according to a news release.</p><p>Renderings released show a three-level “intimate” performances room, with panoramic stage views and dramatic lighting. The venue is also pictured to have a terrace overlooking the United Center, and dedicated community spaces. Audiences will be able to be seated near the stage to create a unique experience. Retail locations, multiple large bars and a flowing open outdoor space are planned.</p><p>It’s all part of the 1901 Project, an effort aimed at transforming over 55 acres around the United Center into an attractive mixed-use neighborhood. Construction officially <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/03/united-center-owners-wirtz-reinsdorf-break-ground-7-billion-1901-project" target="_blank" ><u>kicked off earlier</u></a> this summer. The Music Hall is an addition to a much larger plan to weave together new developments around the United Center.</p><p>Elected officials have called the project the largest private investment on the entries.title: Sox pitcher Mike Vasil throws for first time since Tommy John surgery
entries.summary: <p>Injured right-hander <b>Mike Vasil</b> has been the White Sox’ most visible, boisterous cheerleader all season.</p><p>Before the Sox’ game Friday against the Tigers, his teammates returned the favor.</p><p>Vasil has been sidelined since spring training after tearing the ulnar collateral ligament in his right elbow in a Cactus League game March 14 and having Tommy John surgery April 2. On Friday, he threw a baseball for the first time since the procedure, making 20 tosses from 45 feet on the left-field grass at Rate Field.</p><p>Vasil has been with the Sox all season during his recovery. He became an online sensation for waving a Harry Potter ‘‘wizard wand’’ and donning a pointed wizard hat to help the team celebrate home runs. The Sox even had a wand giveaway night Sept. 4.</p><p>On Friday, Sox players cycled the magic and love back to Vasil. They introduced him on a speaker system as ‘‘Windy City Wizard, Mike Vasil’’ as he sprung out of the dugout, then gathered around a jumping, delighted Vasil as he loosened up and threw.</p><p>‘‘It felt great,’’ Vasil said. ‘‘Shout-out to Dr. [<b>Keith</b>] <b>Meister</b>. A lot of panic this morning. I was in the shower, and I was slightly concerned about if I remembered how to throw a baseball.’’</p><p>The good vibes were more than mechanical.</p><p>‘‘Overall, to have the support of my teammates, too, it really made me emotional,’’ Vasil said. ‘‘Just the fact everyone is behind me and supporting me. I wanted to pitch this year, and it didn’t happen. But to see them out there meant a lot.’’</p><p>The Sox seemed to be conspiring in the clubhouse before Vasil’s session, but they didn’t tell him any details.</p><p>‘‘I didn’t know that was going to happen,’’ Vasil said. ‘‘It was cool to see all of them.’’</p><p>This would have been Vasil’s second season in the majors after he went 5-3 with a 2.50 ERA in 101 innings in a ‘‘Swiss Army knife’’ role with the 102-loss Sox last season. A healthy Vasil figured to fit in with manager <b>Will Venable’s</b> approach of using pitchers in all types of situations.</p><p>‘‘It’s one of the more fun roles in baseball, being able to either go three [innings] in the middle of the game, close or start on any given day,’’ Vasil said. ‘‘It was so fun last year doing that.’’</p><p>Venable was delighted about Vasil’s milestone day and the players’ response.</p><p>‘‘Really proud of ‘Vas’ for getting to point where he’s out here throwing,’’ Venable said. ‘‘It’s really special when you think about what ‘Vas’ has put into this group and, on a daily basis, the energy that he provides our group.</p><p>‘‘That can kind of take a lot out of you, and you forget that he’s rehabbing from Tommy John surgery, which is a really tough thing to do.’’</p><p>Vasil said he hopes to be throwing rehab assignments by next spring, then be activated in late May. There’s still a lot of work ahead.</p><p>He’ll throw again Sunday, then progress slowly to greater distances.</p><p>‘‘Then eventually get on the mound, start throwing bullpen [sessions],’’ Vasil said. ‘‘That’s the long progression, live at-bats. I’m going to do everything in my power to be back right on time.</p><p>‘‘I want to be better than ever. I know I will be.’’</p><h3>Colson in lineup vs. Tigers</h3><p>Shortstop <b>Colson Montgomery</b> was back in the Sox’ lineup Friday, batting eighth against Tigers left-hander <b>Andrew Sears</b>. He responded by hitting a three-run double in the Sox’ six-run first inning.</p><p>Montgomery was hit on the left wrist by a pitch from the Guardians’ <b>Parker Messick</b> on Wednesday in Cleveland. He left that game after being unable to swing the bat and sat out the Sox’ 3-1 victory Thursday against the Tigers.</p><p>Montgomery entered Friday with three hits in 45 at-bats (54 plate appearances) in his last 14 games, a .067 batting average. Two of the hits were homers and one was a double. He had walked five times and been plunked four times.</p>

entries.title: Losing ugly? Sox blow big early lead and fall to Tigers
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> were rolling and raced to a huge early lead Friday against the Tigers at Rate Field.</p><p>Then their pitching staff, including two of their go-to relievers this season, melted down in an ugly 11-8 loss that dropped them a game behind the first-place Guardians in the American League Central.</p><p>It was another defeat that hurt in the South Siders’ playoff push for a division title or an AL wild card. The Sox, now 78-76, are 6-13 since Aug. 29, when they peaked at nine games above .500 (72-63) with a victory against the Twins in Minnesota.</p><p>The Sox staked rookie right-hander David Sandlin to a 8-2 lead in this one, scoring six runs — all unearned — in the first inning and adding two more on Miguel Vargas’ 32nd home run in the third.</p><p>But Sandlin and the Sox’ bullpen couldn’t hold it.</p><p>‘‘That’s tough, no way about it,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘We obviously have a special first inning there and get the lead. [Then Vargas] with a nice homer. And then, yeah, just weren’t able to get any outs.’’</p><p>The Tigers pulled to 8-5 in the fifth on a bases-loaded triple by Kevin McGonigle. Rookie left-hander Hagen Smith relieved Sandlin, who seemed in control through four innings but suddenly couldn’t get an out.</p><p>‘‘I mean, that’s what you ask for as a starting pitcher,’’ Sandlin said. ‘‘Those guys went to work for me, and I couldn’t go to work for them at the end of the day. That’s on me.</p><p>‘‘I’ve got to get more than four innings as a starter and save the bullpen.’’</p><p>Adding to the pain, All-Star outfielder Tristan Peters — who was playing right — hit the wall hard trying to snare McGonigle’s drive and left the game. He suffered a bruised left shoulder and is day-to-day.</p><p>The Sox’ bullpen certainly didn’t save this one, either. The Tigers narrowed their deficit to 8-6 on an RBI double by Hao-Yu Lee against left-hander Chris Murphy in the sixth, then scored five runs in the eighth on the strength of two-run homers by Lee and Riley Greene.</p><p>Lee smacked a two-run shot to right off left-hander Sean Newcomb’s center-cut high fastball to tie the score 8-8 after Newcomb had hit Eduardo Valencia with a pitch on an 0-2 count.</p><p>Newcomb then walked McGonigle. Left-hander Bryan Hudson entered and yielded two singles that put the Tigers ahead 9-8 before Greene launched his 21st homer to complete the rally.</p><p>Newcomb (2-5) was charged the loss, yielding three runs while getting only two outs. He has been scored on in six of his last seven outings, allowing 12 runs in eight innings, after going 11 appearances without yielding a run.</p><p>Hudson, who has been ultra-reliable this season, allowed two runs and four hits in a third of an inning. He hadn’t been scored on in his 11 previous outings spanning 12⅓ innings.</p><p>‘‘We couldn’t slow them down,’’ Venable said. ‘‘It didn’t really matter what spots we put guys in.’’</p><p>After the game, Peters said he ‘‘felt all right and better than initially’’ but was ‘‘really sore.’’ He said the impact from hitting the right-center wall affected ‘‘the back of my shoulder and kind of crunched by shoulders forward.’’</p><p>‘‘I’ve always been a guy that’s going to run into the wall and try to make plays,’’ he said.</p>

entries.title: Michael Busch's caught-stealing caps Cubs' frustrating loss to Reds
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — Outside of Wrigley Field, Cubs left fielder Ian Happ is most productive at Great American Ballpark. He entered the game Friday against the Reds with 18 home runs and a 1.002 OPS there, his best marks at an opponent’s park.</p><p>He added a homer in the third inning, giving him the sixth-most by a visiting player in the stadium’s 24-year history. So why on earth did Michael Busch, who had reached on a walk in the ninth inning, try stealing second base with two outs and Happ representing the tying run?</p><p>After being called safe, Busch was ruled out on a video review, and the Cubs lost 6-4.</p><p>“That was a dumb play,” manager Craig Counsell said. “It was stupid. I’ll take responsibility for it.”</p><p>“That’s just inexcusable on my part,” Busch said. “Gotta make sure if I’m taking that base that I make it 100%. We have a good hitter up in Happ, and that can’t happen.”</p><p>It wasn’t one of the biggest reasons the Cubs lost. Those were right-hander Clay Holmes walking five — including three in the Reds’ game-turning three-run sixth — and the hitters going 2-for-10 with runners in scoring position and leaving nine men on base overall.</p><p>“Can’t walk the leadoff guy there in the sixth inning,” Holmes said. “The walks hurt. The past three outings, I haven’t been efficient.”</p><p>Fortunately for the Cubs, the Phillies also lost, keeping the teams tied for the top spot in the National League wild-card race, with the Cubs holding the tiebreaker. Unfortunately for them, the Padres had a chance to make it a three-way tie late Friday.</p><h3>Swanson returns to action</h3><p>After a rehab assignment that never happened and two simulated games, shortstop Dansby Swanson returned from a strained left oblique. He looked no worse for wear from the start.</p><p>Reds leadoff man Carlos Jorge hit a pop fly down the third-base line that Swanson chased all the way into foul territory next to short left field. He slid on the warning track as he neared the wall but couldn’t make the catch. The official scorer ruled it no play, but that couldn’t have been further from the truth.</p><p>If anyone had concerns about how Swanson’s body would react to real game action, that play should’ve allayed those fears.</p><p>Swanson missed a month with the injury, and his rehab assignment this week with Triple-A Iowa got rained out, forcing the Cubs to get creative. They flew in two minor-leaguers to pitch to him in a sim game Wednesday, during which Swanson also played in the field. He got in another workout Thursday at Wrigley Field before the team left town.</p><p>“We’re our best team when Dansby’s out there,” Counsell said. “We’re our best defensive unit, for sure. The rehab part got screwed up with the weather. We’re excited to have him back.”</p><p>Swanson batted ninth, going 1-for-3 with a walk and a run scored. His hit was an infield single on which he beat the throw from Elly De La Cruz deep in the hole at short.</p><h3>Playoff rotation can wait</h3><p>With only eight games left in the regular season after Friday and a playoff berth likely in their future, the Cubs are starting to think about how they’d like to line up their postseason rotation. But thinking is all that they’re doing.</p><p>“We’ve got a lot to accomplish before that,” Counsell said. “Do you start thinking about those things? Absolutely, you have to think about them. But my experience is that those decisions change many times. So you just kind of position yourself for possibilities.”</p><p>Counsell refuses to look at much beyond the game at hand.</p><p>“Worry about today; that’s all we can do today,” he said. “I know that’s coachspeak, but it’s how you have to work as athletes and coaches. Getting ahead of ourselves for those things is useless.”</p>
